name: Marco Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential. What fills a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and have managed six people preparing export documents for a large equipment maker for five years. I check product codes, destination rules and delivery certificates before a shipment goes. I use AI every day to spot mismatched codes, then I read the source document because a wrong certificate can strand a container. I like the moment a shipment clears; I dislike telling the warehouse that our paperwork held up their work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and how many choices could you afford if the role changed?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife, Inez, works for a gardening business, and our children are eight and fourteen. We have a mortgage, about four months of expenses saved, and my pay is typical for a manager here. There are some similar export offices nearby. I have a bachelor’s degree and know this work reasonably well; outside work I repair our family’s bicycles, but nobody has paid me for that yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a code checker saves time, but someone still signs the certificate. The warehouse should not wait on a clever draft with the wrong destination.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My role should hold, though Inez’s gardening hours fall in winter. Four months saved can cover a short season, but we still have a mortgage due every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep my morning code check with the shipping clerk and verify AI flags against the destination rule before signing. In the first year Inez and I would keep transferring 100 monthly into savings only when her gardening hours are full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the winter budget, though work itself looks steady. A few saved minutes do not change the seasons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which mistake would bother you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A destination code on the wrong country’s form would bother me most. A container with the wrong country code could sit at the port while the warehouse asks why I signed its export certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not put more into savings now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inez’s winter hours can shrink. I would not build a savings target on pay that may not arrive.

say: I’d keep a **person signing** each export certificate after checking its destination code.
A code draft must match the **destination rule**.
think: My **manager role** continues and should pay its usual wage in a plateau.
Inez’s **winter hours** can tighten the mortgage budget despite four months saved.
do: Keep the **morning code check** and verify AI flags against destination rules.
Save **100 monthly** only when Inez’s gardening hours are full.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about seasonal household income.
S0.quote: A container with the wrong country code could sit at the port while the warehouse asks why I signed its export certificate.
fieldNote: He uses **AI daily** but signs only after source checks.
Winter gardening hours could **shrink household income** enough to pressure the mortgage.
Savings depend on **full gardening hours**, not a promised amount.

steps.text: Keep morning export-code checks and verify AI flags against destination rules
Transfer 100 monthly to savings only when Inez’s gardening hours are full

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team that writing and checking certificates are exactly what the new software will do. I’d show the warehouse both the saved time and any stranded shipments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We might need fewer document staff, and the company could merge my team with another one. I can use the tools, but one manager over two desks could mean my wage goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This quarter I’d test AI on eighty old export packets, counting the wrong destination codes the shipping clerk finds. In the first year I’d take a paid course on the new customs screen and offer simple bicycle repairs on Saturdays only after five neighbours agree to pay and Inez can cover the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about a merged team. The bicycle work is an experiment, not a second salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you charge for a bicycle repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d quote for the part and one hour, then keep a record of the actual time. If five neighbours will not pay, I will not buy more tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why test the customs screen yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the failure cases and I can learn the screen quickly. If my team gets smaller, I want the error record to travel with the decision.

say: I’d show **wrong destination codes** beside time saved before any staffing change.
Certificate writing and checking are **exposed tasks** across our team.
think: A team merger might cost **my manager wage**.
Tool skill cannot guarantee a job when **one desk remains**.
do: Test **eighty old packets** for destination errors.
Complete **paid customs training** and take bicycle jobs only after five neighbours agree to pay and Inez covers the children.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the desk and cautious about repair income.
S1.quote: If five neighbours will not pay, I will not buy more tools.
fieldNote: He ties adoption to **stranded shipments**, not speed alone.
He sees **his own wage** exposed by a merger.
Bicycle work requires **paying customers and childcare**, without speculative tool spending.

steps.text: Test AI certificates against eighty old export packets
Complete the paid company course on the new customs screen
Take Saturday bicycle repairs only after five neighbours agree to pay and Inez covers children

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for written closure dates and a named person to fix a bad export certificate. I’d tell the warehouse not to trust a form just because it was produced quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could do the coding and checking that make up my day, so I expect my post to go. Inez’s gardening and my small bicycle orders are hands-on until robots arrive around 2031, but neither would cover the mortgage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week Inez and I would pause our planned car replacement and keep the deposit in cash. Before 2028 I’d ask a bicycle shop about posted paid repair work and keep only bicycle orders that cover parts; in the first year after AGI arrives, I’d take a posted shop job only if its written wage covers my mortgage share and the shifts leave a parent home after school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed by the speed. Four months saved gives me a little time, not a new trade wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a repair shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have repaired family bikes, but I would not put our mortgage behind a shop lease without a book of paying customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your fourteen-year-old?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a paid apprenticeship is worth looking at alongside college, but I would not choose their studies to solve my job problem. I would show the actual wages and let my child decide.

say: I’d seek **written closure dates** before the export desk is handed to software.
A bad certificate needs a **named repair contact**.
think: Gardening and bicycle repair face **2031 robots** and cannot replace my wage yet.
do: Pause the **car replacement** and keep its deposit available.
Ask about **posted bicycle repair** and move only with written mortgage-share pay and a parent home after school.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by the short runway.
S2.quote: I would not put our mortgage behind a shop lease without a book of paying customers.
fieldNote: His desk tasks face **2028 AGI** before 2031 hands-on robots.
He refuses a **shop lease** without paid demand.
A paid repair role requires **written wages** and school-compatible shifts.

steps.text: Pause the planned car replacement and hold its deposit in cash
Ask a bicycle shop about posted paid repair vacancies before 2028
Take posted bicycle repair after 2028 only with written mortgage-share wages and parent home after school

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years is enough for the company to show the export team which posts actually go and when. I’d want a real wage on any suggested transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build a list of paying bicycle customers while my export salary still comes in. The shop’s quotes and bookings face AGI in 2031, and hands-on repairs face robots around 2034, so I know it is a bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next spring I’d take ten paid bicycle jobs a month only if Inez can cover Saturday childcare and the parts are paid for up front. I’d keep a log of parts and time, then apply for an advertised shop mechanic post before 2031 only if its wage covers my mortgage share; after AGI arrives, I’d stay only while paid hands-on work is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but five years lets me find out if customers return. I would not leave my manager wage for a stack of friendly promises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take work from a neighbour who wants a free favour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might help a friend once, but I would not count it as business income. The parts and an hour of my Saturday need a price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Inez cannot cover Saturdays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take fewer orders or do repairs when she is off. I will not leave the younger child alone to make a bicycle plan look bigger.

say: I’d ask for **post dates and wages** before the export team changes.
The export team should see **real openings** before anyone is transferred.
think: Paid bicycle orders might build a **bridge income** while my export salary still arrives.
Shop quotes face **2031 AGI** before 2034 repair robots.
do: Take **ten paid repairs** only with Inez’s childcare and parts paid up front.
Apply for an **advertised mechanic post** only with pay covering my mortgage share.
Keep **repair work** after 2031 only while paid hands-on jobs remain.
feel: I feel **anxious** but can count returning customers.
S3.quote: I would not leave my manager wage for a stack of friendly promises.
fieldNote: The bicycle shop’s **booking work** faces AGI before robot repair.
His family schedule and **upfront parts** limit the side work.

steps.text: Take ten paid bicycle orders monthly only if Inez covers childcare and customers pay parts upfront
Record paid repair hours and parts for each bicycle
Apply for advertised mechanic work before 2031 only if wages cover mortgage share

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade lets families reduce debt and employers offer honest wages for changing work. I would not tell my team a certificate by itself is a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 in 2036, with our children older and the mortgage perhaps smaller. If our wages hold, I could build a larger reserve and have a real repair-customer list; yet the export desk and shop booking face 2036 AGI, with repair robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January 2027 Inez and I would transfer 180 monthly to savings only when both wages hold and the mortgage stays current. I’d take paid bicycle orders on Saturdays only if ten monthly bookings actually come in, and apply for a posted repair role before 2036 only if the wage covers my mortgage share; after AGI arrives, I’d stay only while human repair work is paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy but able to plan. A decade gives us time to see whether repair work has paying customers instead of just compliments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you borrow against the house for a repair van?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would buy tools only from money the repairs actually earn, and I would keep the mortgage out of a new venture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say learning to fix a thing is useful, but they should look at actual wages and future changes. I would not choose a trade for them.

say: A certificate alone is not a **job offer**.
A decade could let families **reduce debt** before changing work.
think: I could build a **larger reserve** if wages hold.
Export and shop booking face **2036 AGI** before 2039 repair robots.
do: Save **180 monthly** only while wages and mortgage payments hold.
Take **paid Saturday orders** only with real demand, then seek repair work covering my mortgage share.
Stay in **bicycle repair** after 2036 only while human work remains paid.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but able to test demand.
S4.quote: I would keep the mortgage out of a new venture.
fieldNote: He uses **paid orders** to judge a repair business.
Savings depend on **both wages** and a current mortgage.
He recognizes **2036 desk exposure** even in a repair shop.

steps.text: Transfer 180 monthly into savings only while both wages hold and mortgage stays current

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my export desk could close before bicycle repairs pay enough to matter. Written notice, an actual paid shop vacancy and a mortgage-covering wage would help. I would not ask Inez to carry the house on seasonal gardening wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who pays when an export form is wrong and a container sits at the port. A quick certificate is still slow when it sends a shipment to the wrong place.

headlineQuote: A quick certificate is still slow when it sends a shipment to the wrong place.
portrait: **Marco**, 43, is an experienced export-documents manager with a bachelor’s degree.
Typical pay and **four months saved** support the mortgage, though Inez’s gardening income is seasonal.
He uses **AI daily** but checks destination rules before signing.
He tests **paid bicycle repairs** without borrowing against the family home.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his export desk before bicycle repairs earn a viable wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a posted paid repair vacancy and mortgage-covering wages would help.
